threads_text: Google DeepMind just announced Genie 4, a world model that builds interactive scenes in real time, now with its own sound, music and characters that talk back. You steer it by typing, like changing the weather or adding a person. Would you rather play a game made this way or watch a movie made this way?

site_article.headline: Google DeepMind unveils Genie 4, a real time world model that generates its own audio
site_article.dek: The research preview adds ambient sound, music and character dialogue to simulated worlds that users steer with plain language.
site_article.summary: Google DeepMind announced Genie 4 on October 27, 2026, a world model that generates interactive scenes in real time along with native audio. It is available to trusted testers first, with Google AI Ultra subscribers and Gemini API partners to follow.
site_article.seo_title: Google DeepMind Genie 4 adds native audio to world model
site_article.seo_description: Google DeepMind announced Genie 4, a real time world model with native sound and dialogue, in research preview for trusted testers.
site_article.answer_summary: Genie 4 is Google DeepMind's newest world model. It creates interactive scenes in real time with generated sound and speech, and it is in research preview for trusted testers.
site_article.hero_alt: Promotional image for Google DeepMind's Genie 4 world model showing a generated scene.

paragraphs.text: On October 27, 2026, Google DeepMind announced Genie 4, a world model that generates interactive scenes in real time and lets people steer them with plain language. Google described the release as a research preview, and it is going first to a limited group of trusted testers.

The headline addition is sound. According to Google, every world Genie 4 builds now comes with audio generated on the fly, including ambient sound, music and interactive dialogue, so characters inside a scene can talk and respond to the user. SQ Magazine and NPowerUser both report that DeepMind calls it its first real-time world model to generate audio natively.

Users start an event and then change it while it runs. Google lists moving the camera, changing the weather and adding characters as examples of natural language instructions the model accepts. NPowerUser reports that keyboard input handles navigation and camera control, while typed prompts handle edits, and that the model adapts each prompt to fit the scene already on screen.

Genie 4 leans on Google's Gemini family. Google says Gemini Omni grounds each simulation in real world appearance and behavior, while other Gemini models supply the reasoning needed to keep scenes coherent. According to SQ Magazine and Unite.AI, Gemini 3.8 Flash runs as a guiding agent that breaks goals into steps, checks incoming frames and revises its plan when a user steps in.

DeepMind also points to better physics, including aerodynamics and collisions, and to more natural human motion, with simulated people reacting to their surroundings and to user direction, according to Unite.AI and NPowerUser.

Early testers span several fields. Unite.AI and SQ Magazine report that filmmakers are using Genie 4 for previsualization, photojournalists are testing whether archival photos can be turned into explorable simulations, and game developers are using it for rapid prototyping. SQ Magazine reports that Google DeepMind engineer Diego Rivas said real time generation is most useful for ideation and storyboarding.

Robotics is another target. Google frames simulation as a way to build safe training environments for robots and AI agents. Unite.AI describes an experiment in which Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini Robotics were paired with Genie 4 to rehearse a scenario where Apptronik's Apollo humanoid played checkers, and SQ Magazine reports that the Argon model split tasks into steps and passed them to Genie 4 as text captions.

Google says Genie 4 is coming soon to Google AI Ultra subscribers through Project Genie and to early access partners in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. A waitlist for Project Genie is open, according to SQ Magazine and Unite.AI. Both outlets also report that every video and audio clip the model produces carries an invisible SynthID watermark.

Google has listed known weaknesses. According to SQ Magazine and Unite.AI, visual details and object permanence can drift during longer sessions or after complex edits, and real time audio accuracy, legible text inside generated worlds, spatial accuracy and long term consistency all remain open research problems.

Adding live sound and speech moves world models closer to something that feels like a playable scene rather than a silent video clip. The listed limitations, especially drift over longer sessions, suggest the model is better suited for short sketches and rehearsals than for finished productions for now, which matches how Google is positioning the early testers.
The next marker is the Google AI Ultra rollout in Project Genie, which will show how long paying subscribers can actually run a session and how well the native audio holds up outside curated demos.
